Convergent Integration Pairing Tool

QUAL — IPA Themes (15 items)

Pharmacological-historical
Generational framing of own use as modest experimentation; 'smoked a bit of old-fashioned grass...probably dropped acid a couple of times'
Source: GET 3.1/4.1
Moral/linguistic threshold
Consistent terminology 'substance misusers' rather than 'addicts,' implying threshold-based construal where use itself is unremarkable
Source: GET 4.2
Humanizing/normalization
'People around the world really have the same...kinds of emotions. They get depressed, they get anxious, they take drugs, they don't take drugs'
Source: GET 4.2
Legal/contextual
Real-time revision of legal-illegal construct for alcohol; 'it depends on...your age...legally obtained if you're of age...illegally obtained if you're underage. So maybe put that as a 3'
Source: GET 4.1
Pharmacological
Pharmacological nuance on alcohol; 'it changes. [I] Think it starts out stimulating and ends up as a depressant'
Source: GET 4.1
Threshold/pathology
Threshold qualifier that consequences emerge only 'with overuse'
Source: GET 4.2
Evolving-evidence
Awareness of hallucinogen research for depression and PTSD
Source: GET 4.1
Social-context
Alcohol described as 'one of the most social' substances yet linked to isolation as use progresses; touches RQ1b where construct organizes users
Source: GET 4.3
Class/function
Class-based functional framing; productive use linked with lower SES while recreational use construed as socially inclusive
Source: GET 4.3
Cultural
Identification of psychedelic use within Native cultures
Source: GET 4.4
Pharmacological
Pharmacological-perceptual distinction; 'MDMA and mushroom...they're more mind-altering, people are tripping' contrasted with 'Alcohol...mood-altering actually'
Source: GET 4.1
Pathology-threshold
Preference for 'overusing' over 'overdose,' reflecting threshold-based reasoning
Source: GET 4.2
Structural/economic
Spontaneous identification of economic accessibility as an organizing dimension of substances
Source: GET 4.3
Evolving-evidence
Recognition that cannabis and psychedelics are moving into legitimate therapeutic realms
Source: GET 4.1
Cultural
Critique of American drinking-age policy from a European perspective; supervised exposure to alcohol at 16 construed as promoting responsibility; consistent with Addo (2018)
Source: GET 4.4

QUAL — IPA Themes (39 items)

A: Humanizing
Consistent use of 'substance misuser,' distancing clients from pathological labels; prefix 'mis-' implies threshold where use itself is unremarkable
Source: GET 4, 4.2
A: Humanizing
Placed substance use within ordinary variability of human experience; 'They get depressed, they get anxious, they take drugs, they don't take drugs...they love their families, they don't love their families'
Source: GET 4, 4.2
A: Humanizing
Recognized incarcerated client's sales abilities despite criminal history; strengths-based, person-first construal; 'He could have sold Coles to Newcastle!'
Source: GET 4, 4.2
A: Humanizing
Linguistic oscillation between 'had a substance misuse problem' (condition) and 'are substance misusers' (identity); shifts between conditional and identity-based framings
Source: GET 4, 4.2
B: Loss/Proximity
First people grid construct was mortality ('dead or alive'), transformed into avoidance-versus-closeness; the dead held close through grief while some living kept at distance
Source: GET 1, 1.2
B: Loss/Proximity
Advocacy for murdered friend Marno against legal system's dehumanizing language; 'In the court documents, some lawyer referred to her as just a waitress'
Source: GET 1, 1.2
B: Loss/Proximity
Memorialized Marno through cultural and spiritual meaning-making; 'the Egyptians had an ancient belief that if someone says your name, you never...your soul never dies'
Source: GET 1, 1.3
B: Loss/Proximity
Teenagers unknowingly exposed to laced drugs construed as victims of market exploitation; people framed through forces acting upon them
Source: GET 1, 1.1
C: Self-Positioning
Generational framing of substance knowledge within 1960s cultural context; experimentation as historically contextualized and modest
Source: GET 3, 3.1
C: Self-Positioning
Generational cohort's substance knowledge as cultural value; 'We knew a lot, because we felt we should'
Source: GET 3, 3.1
C: Self-Positioning
Music industry exposure demystified identity of person who uses substances, eliminating relational distance between counselor and client
Source: GET 1, 1.4
C: Self-Positioning
Fatigue during grid elicitation produced unmodulated evaluative language ('Hannah's an arrogant cow'); sustained empathic framing depends on cognitive resources
Source: GET 5, 5.5

Empathy for what clients lose in recovery from stimulant use; 'You're talking about dealing with not feeling stimulated all the time. And not have that immediate...Rush of dopamine'
Source: GET 4, 4.2
A: Humanizing
Conditional framework for consequences; substances do not carry inherent negative outcomes; pathology emerges only 'with overuse'
Source: GET 4, 4.2

Refused to generalize about sedatives because she lacked clinical experience; 'I haven't treated a lot of people that are coming specifically off of sedatives, so I don't know how to speak to that'
Source: GET 4, 4.2

Rejected hierarchy with visceral discomfort; 'I don't do this thing where I'm better than...You know that feels icky to me to even say that'

Existential confusion about differential outcomes; 'I was abusing the substance equally...but I didn't understand why I could stop, and they couldn't'; labeled as survivor's guilt
Source: GET 1, 1.2

Gendered social dynamics in addiction; women become addicted faster and are more socially influenced by men to begin using

Race absent from clinical experience as a factor; 'I don't think race, I don't...in my experience, I don't see race as a factor'

QUAL — IPA Themes (30 items)

Nonlinear pathway
Career traversed English degree, 18 years in the music industry, and 11 years as stay-at-home mother; framed non-clinical background as asset exposing her to 'all kinds of people from all kinds of backgrounds'
Source: GET 2.1
Credential accumulation
Ongoing degree accumulation as professional habit; 'three more degrees' completed and a sixth planned; self-correction suggests she has lost count
Source: GET 2.2
Self-positioning re: substances
Generational framing of personal experimentation; 'I confess, I smoked a bit of old-fashioned grass and probably took quaaludes a few times'; mock-guilty acknowledgment without pathologizing
Source: GET 3.1
Credential question (indirect)
Supervisory narrative about trainee assigned to anorexic clients despite visible characteristic mismatch; 'you've lost your credibility instantly'; reveals awareness that credibility is a constructed perception
Source: GET 3.2
Theoretical orientation as identity
Harm reduction as conscious, explicit identity declaration; 'I take a harm reduction stance'; affective attachment to specific theorists (Tatarski, Peele)
Source: GET 5.1
Cross-participant pattern
Professional identity as ongoing project assembled through credential accumulation, comparison to ideal models; absence of recovery prevents anchoring in singular transformative narrative
Source: GET 2
Self-constructed pathway
Graduate program offered no substance use training; advocated for voluntary, unpaid second internship; 'I kind of went in there and made it work for me, actually'
Source: GET 2.1
Cooperative formative experience
Developed alongside supervisor Robin who was also new to the role; cooperative arrangement lacking clear hierarchy; likely informed egalitarian therapeutic stance
Source: GET 2.1
Education as legitimacy
Elicited 'educated versus non-educated' construct during grid; hesitant to acknowledge its presence; introduced nuance that intelligence exists independently of formal education ('she's a smart cookie')
Source: GET 2.2
Ideal Self refinement
Initially aligned aspirations with clinical supervisors, then self-corrected; 'I also never want to be in a clinical, supervisory role... Maybe the colleague'; rejected hierarchical role, aligned Ideal Self with peer
Source: GET 2.3
Leadership reframe
Reframed leadership as service; 'I strive to be as a leader for my clients'; recognized necessity of leadership in group work while rejecting positional authority
Source: GET 2.3
Self in relation to addiction
Liminal substance history translated into therapeutic stance; 'we' language as refusal to other clients; 'when we get ourselves in these positions, when we are actively using' [also serves RQ3]
Source: GET 3.1
Alternative credential pathway
Identified colleague whose parents were both in recovery; validated familial proximity as legitimate alternative credential; 'that's what makes her a good counselor'
Source: GET 3.1
Credential question (direct)
Estimated one in five clients directly asked whether she was in recovery; persistent challenges to professional authority from clients
Source: GET 3.2
Incidental entry
Encountered field through internship placement at adolescent group-care facility; 'never heard of substance use counseling at the time'
Source: GET 2.1
Education as legitimacy
Explicitly linked credibility to formal credentials and licensure; 'Professional credibility in terms of education...certification basis, or licensure'; educational attainment distinguished him in regional context with many entry-level practitioners
Source: GET 2.2
Limits of credentials
Recognized gap between credentials and competence; 'Two different CRSs with the same education. One is a little bit more professional'; 'the papers that you show me, like, that's something, but...'
Source: GET 2.2
Developmental self-assessment
'Advanced for where I'm at, but generally, like, still intermediate'; contextualized within six to seven years of experience; compared self against 50-year Hazelden veteran
Source: GET 2.3
Ideal Self as aspiration
Named Ideal Self as 'a later on type of thing'; 'Always trying to kind of push forward versus being stagnant'; 'Hope that never changes'; aspires to remain in ongoing becoming
Source: GET 2.3
Recovery as social capital
Observed recovery history functioning as social capital in recovery-dominant workplace culture; deliberated about self-disclosure across institutional settings; engaged in online discussions with counselors from varying recovery backgrounds
Source: GET 3.2
Theoretical orientation as identity
Distanced self from disease model; defined professional standing through evidence-based biopsychosocial orientation; theoretical commitment served as primary lens for evaluating others
Source: GET 5.1
Delayed pathway
Wanted to help others for years before formal training; delayed by family responsibilities and husband's military career; credential trajectory spanning a decade from associate's through master's in Social Work
Source: GET 2.1
Training gaps
Acknowledged limitations in formal training; 'I wasn't specifically trained on modalities like CBT... There's a lot of Motivational Interviewing'; framed ongoing development as supplement to credentials
Source: GET 2.2
Self-positioning re: substances
Applied clinical lens retrospectively to own past substance use; distinguished former recreational use from current nicotine dependence; non-defensive self-examination
Source: GET 3.1
Parallel credential challenge
Drew parallel between non-recovering credential question and work with military populations; 'I only have the experience, again, secondhand. Because my husband and my children are in the military'
Source: GET 3.1
Legitimacy anxiety
Described fear of being unable to relate as 'the biggest fear of mine' early in career; fear revolved around relational capacity; intensified by prevalence of recovering counselors in training program
Source: GET 3.2
Fear resolution
Discovered challenges occurred less frequently than feared; 'I can't count on both hands how many times I was asked if I'm in recovery'; 'I've been only asked twice in four years'
Source: GET 3.3
Redefinition of experience
Reframed family-of-origin exposure as alternative experiential credential; 'It has grown my confidence... I have lived experienced with different kinds, if that makes sense'
Source: GET 3.3
Marginalized identity positioning
Positioned self alongside colleague of color rather than White supervisor; drew on immigrant background as marginalized-group membership; 'How I came in technically part of a marginalized group... Tom's dominant'
Source: GET 3
Theoretical orientation as identity
Grounded approach in Motivational Interviewing as non-judgmental framework; self-corrected from 'cultural competence' to 'cultural humility'; 'That's the ideal'
Source: GET 5.1
